standard.title: Literary devices and word play
standard.description: examine how literary devices including figurative language, deliberate word play and rhythm can be used for particular effects in poetry and literary texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students discuss how literary devices including rhythm and onomatopoeia enhance meaning (AC9E3LE04). They have not yet examined how figurative language, deliberate word play and rhythm produce particular effects in poetry and literary texts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify figurative language (simile, personification, alliteration), deliberate word play (puns, ambiguity) and rhythm in poetry and literary texts, and examine how each produces specific effects on meaning and reader response.

nodes.label: Figurative language — simile, personification, alliteration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify similes, personification and alliteration in texts and explain the specific effect each creates.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example each of simile, personification or alliteration and explain the effect it creates.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss a range of figurative language devices across poetry and literary texts — simile, personification, alliteration — explaining how each device produces a specific effect: comparison, animation, sound pattern.
wider: Compare how the same figurative device (e.g. simile) is used for different effects in two different texts — one creating beauty, one creating horror
Examine figurative language in First Nations Australian poetry, including how imagery draws on Country, seasonal cycles and cultural knowledge for its effects

response_modes.reason: Recognition of figurative language and ability to explain its effect is built through encountering many examples across many texts. Students who have only seen one or two examples apply the device labels superficially.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Figurative language across genres and cultural contexts — especially First Nations Australian poetic traditions — is rich territory. The range of effects achievable through the same device is wide and genuinely engaging.
success_criteria: Can identify and name at least two different figurative devices in a text
Can explain the specific effect of at least one device, not just identify it

nodes.label: Word play — puns, ambiguity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify deliberate word play including puns and ambiguity, and explain why the author made the choice.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a pun or deliberately ambiguous word and explain the double meaning the author is using.
nodes.typical_width: Identify deliberate word play across a range of texts — puns, jokes, deliberate use of ambiguity — and explain both the double meaning and the effect it creates: humour, irony, mystery.
wider: Collect examples of word play from a range of sources (poetry, advertisements, jokes, books) and categorise by type and effect
Examine how word play in poetry creates multiple layers of meaning simultaneously and discuss why this is a valued poetic technique
success_criteria: Can identify a pun and explain both meanings it activates
Understands that word play is deliberate — the author chose to create the double meaning

nodes.label: Rhythm and sound effects
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify rhythm and sound patterns in poetry and literary texts and explain the effect each creates on meaning and reader experience.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a rhythmic or sound pattern in a poem (e.g. regular beat, alliteration pattern) and explain one effect it has on the reader.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss how rhythm — regular beat, varied pace, line length — and sound devices — alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia — work together in poetry to create effects of pace, mood, emphasis and pleasure.
wider: Compare the rhythm of a traditional children's poem with a contemporary free-verse poem and explain how the different rhythmic choices produce different reading experiences
Explore how First Nations Australian song poetry uses rhythm and sound patterning for cultural, ceremonial and storytelling purposes
success_criteria: Can identify a rhythm or sound pattern in a poem and explain one effect it has
Does not describe sound patterns as just 'nice sounding' — can connect the pattern to a specific effect
